summary: SE-led deep dive on KV cache eviction/paging and prefix-reuse with emphasis on long-context workloads. Discussed root causes (cache pressure from high concurrency and variable sequence lengths), heuristics for eviction, and mitigations: pinning frequently reused prefixes, adjusting cache partitioning, and tuning max_cached_tokens. Decided SE to reproduce locally and run benchmarks; security docs and pilot pricing to be shared.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to focus on KV cache behavior you reported - eviction and paging under long context and high concurrency. Ethan and Ravi from our perf team are on to go deep.
[00:12] Sofia Ramirez: Thanks Maya. We started seeing more cache evictions last month after rolling out the 16k context model for the summarization pipeline. Latency spikes when user sessions hit long histories, and sometimes we see weird prefix reuse where the same initial prompt isn't yielding cache hits.
[00:25] Ethan Brooks: Got it. Can you describe the traffic pattern - are there lots of short sessions interleaved with a few very long ones?
[00:30] Daniel Kwan: Yeah, mostly. 80% are short (200-600 tokens) but 5-10% are 8k-16k. Concurrency ain't huge, maybe 100 p50, but bursts to 400 during business hours.
[00:45] Ravi Nair: Those tail long sequences plus bursts are exactly the kind of pressure that can cause eviction thrashing. Our KV cache is LRU-ish but with partitioning across GPU shards. If one shard gets a heavy long-context stream it can evict entries that other concurrent shards still want.
[01:02] Sofia Ramirez: We also noticed paging events on the logs - it says "cache page out" then a read - is that normal?
[01:10] Ethan Brooks: We have two mechanisms: in-memory KV and an optional spill-to-disk/page mechanism when the in-memory bucket is exhausted. Paging is expected if the hot set exceeds the cache allocation. But frequent paging hurts latency.
[01:20] Alex Gomez: The paging messages line up with a 300-600ms tail latency for those requests.
[01:25] Ethan Brooks: That makes sense. Paging is synchronous on a miss currently - so you get the penalty. Good news: we can reduce occurrences by tuning a few knobs.
[01:33] Maya Chen: Right, and there are software mitigations and config ones. Software: prefix pinning, smarter eviction policy, and adaptive partition resizing. Config: increase max_cached_tokens, reserve slots for long-context sessions, or use dedicated pools.
[01:46] Priya Shah: Dedicated pools - what are the tradeoffs? We are sensitive about cost but need predictable latency for SLAs.
[01:53] Ethan Brooks: Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools so you don't get interference. It costs more up front but reduces noisy-neighbor eviction. Also gives control over allocation size for the KV cache.
[02:04] Daniel Kwan: Is there a way to pin prefixes per customer? Some of our users have repeated system prompts they reuse across sessions. If we could persist those prefixes across calls we'd get a lot of reuse.
[02:14] Ravi Nair: Yes, prefix pinning is supported - you can mark specific KV entries as non-evictable or with higher priority. The caveat is you'll need to budget tokens for pinned prefixes. For a 16k model, pinned 1-2k tokens per high-value prefix add up.
[02:30] Sofia Ramirez: How does prefix reuse interact with batching? We batch a lot to save cost.
[02:35] Ethan Brooks: Batching can help amortize work but if batch mixes sessions with different prefixes, you might lose reuse because the cache keys include prefix context. Our batching layer tries to co-batch similar prefixes when possible, but with extreme diversity it won't always align.
[02:50] Alex Gomez: We saw cases where micro-batching (smaller batch size) actually improved cache hit rate because it grouped by user. But that increased GPU overhead.
[02:58] Ethan Brooks: Right, this is the latency vs cost tradeoff. Another approach is prefetching - if you know a long session is starting, warm the KV for common prefixes. That reduces first-request latency.
[03:12] Daniel Kwan: You mentioned partitioning earlier - can you explain how partitions are sized and if we can reconfigure?
[03:18] Ravi Nair: Partitions correspond to GPU-local cache slices. We default to equal-sized partitions, but for uneven traffic you can set static weights or enable adaptive resizing. Adaptive monitors per-partition hit/miss and shifts token budget between partitions. It helps but adds some background compaction overhead.
[03:34] Sofia Ramirez: Any recommendations for the numbers we'd tweak? max_cached_tokens, partition count, eviction window?
[03:40] Ethan Brooks: For your distribution (majority short, small tail of long), start with: increase max_cached_tokens by 30% on the busiest pool, set min_pinned_slots for known prefixes (e.g., 10 slots of 512 tokens), and enable adaptive_partitioning. Also set eviction_window to 5k tokens for long sessions so the system favors older long-context entries slightly longer.
[04:02] Maya Chen: We'll put those into a config recipe. Another angle: quantization and memory footprint. If you use 8-bit quantization it reduces KV storage per key?
[04:12] Ravi Nair: Quantization mainly affects model weights and KV memory layout can also be compressed. We support compressed KV payloads which save about 30-40% depending on tokenizer and hidden-size. That can defer paging. But note decompression adds CPU overhead on the host.
[04:29] Sofia Ramirez: Hmm - we have limited CPU headroom on our infra nodes. Decompression cost might be non-trivial.
[04:34] Ethan Brooks: True - it's a tradeoff. For many customers the sweet spot is a mixed strategy: compress only infrequently accessed entries and keep hot prefixes uncompressed. We can automate that via a hotness threshold.
[04:46] Daniel Kwan: You mentioned LRU-ish eviction. Are there smarter algorithms available - e.g., LFU or a hybrid?
[04:52] Ravi Nair: We experimented with LRU+frequency heuristics (an approximate LFU) that stabilizes against thrashing. Hybrid LFU prevents short-lived bursts from evicting moderately popular items. It does need counters and more memory but reduces churn.
[05:06] Alex Gomez: Are there any observable signals we should track to know eviction is the root cause vs something else?
[05:11] Ethan Brooks: Key metrics: KV hit rate, paging events per second, eviction rate, and per-request tail latency correlating with page-in time. Also look at distribution of key sizes and the number of unique prefixes per minute. We'll share a dashboard template.
[05:25] Sofia Ramirez: Yep, those map to what we saw. We also have curious behavior where a reused prefix still misses after a while - could that be hash collisions?
[05:33] Ravi Nair: Unlikely but possible in pathological cases. More often it's prefix normalization mismatch - whitespace, different tokens due to client-side preprocessing, or minor punctuation changes. We recommend canonicalizing prompts before sending.
[05:47] Priya Shah: On security: if we pin prefixes, does that change data residency or compliance posture?
[05:52] Ethan Brooks: Pinning is a runtime allocation; it doesn't change storage policy. If you enable disk spill, you can opt-out of spill-to-disk or require encryption with your KMS key. For Private/VPC deployments, you control where cached pages land. We'll attach the KMS and VPC docs in the follow-up.
[06:10] Maya Chen: Let's capture concrete next steps: Ethan to reproduce locally and gather logs, Maya to send security docs + pricing, and schedule the benchmarking session. Anything else?
[06:18] Sofia Ramirez: We'll share our sequence length histogram and a sample anonymized request set.
[06:22] Daniel Kwan: Also we'll try prefix canonicalization on a small batch to see immediate gains.
[06:26] Ethan Brooks: Perfect. We'll also try a prefix-pin experiment on our test pool to quantify the hit-rate delta.
[06:31] Maya Chen: Great, thanks everyone. We'll reconvene after Ethan's repro.
[06:36] Priya Shah: Thanks.
[06:38] [Call ends]
